title: Lab 4 – Thyroid
html:
Source: LP 4.pdf – 11 pages

Goiter- WHO staging #1

  • Grade 1 = small goiter, can’t be observed with the head in a normal position (only with the
  • head in hyperextension), but it can be palpated.
  • Grade 2 = moderate goiter, visible with the head in normal position, palpable, does not extend
  • beyond the external branch of SCM muscle.
  • Grade 3 = one or both lobes extend beyond the external branch of SCM muscle, visible from
  • 10 m distance ± pressure symptoms in the neck.
  • Grade 4 = huge goiter, extends inferiorly-> substernal goiter and superiorly toward the
  • mandible, it totally deforms the neck and it can be “seen” from behind+ important pressure
  • symptoms in the neck.
  • Hyperthyroidism- causes
  • 1. Thyrotoxicosis with hyperthyroidism
  • • Graves’ disease
  • • Toxic multinodular goiter
  • • Toxic adenoma
  • • Iodine-induced (Jod–Basedow)- amiodarone (contains 37% I), radiographic contrast media
  • • TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
  • 2. Thyrotoxicosis without hyperthyroidism
  • • Thyrotoxicosis factitious (iatrogenic or voluntary ingestion of thyroxine or thyroid hormones)
  • • Subacute thyroiditis (viral etiology)
  • • Thyroiditis with transient thyrotoxicosis (e.g. Hashytoxicosis)
  • • Ectopic thyroid tissue (struma ovarii= teratoma containing thyroid tissue)
  • Hyperthyroidism- clinical picture
  • 1. General manifestations: ↑ basal metabolic rate, ↑body temperature (37–37.5 °C), heat
  • intolerance and sweating, fatigue, and weakness.
  • 2. Nervous system: emotional lability, nervousness, irritability, insomnia, restlessness, tremor
  • of the eyelid/ togue/ hands (fine, rhythmic), hyperkinesia, hyperreflexia
  • 3. Cardiovascular system: palpitations (increased cardiac output+ tachycardia), loud heart
  • sounds, functional systolic murmurs, divergent BP formula (↓ DBP, ↑SBP), hyperkinetic
  • cardiovascular syndrome, congestive heart failure.
  • !!Cardiac arrhythmias- almost invariably supraventricular: extrasystoles, atrial fibrillation, and
  • paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.
  • 4. Digestive manifestations: ↑appetite but with weight loss (↑ basal metabolic rate), ↑gut
  • motility, hepatic dysfunction (particularly when thyrotoxicosis is severe).

5. Muscular effects: proximal muscle weakness, respiratory muscle weakness-> dyspnea on #2

  • exertion
  • 6. Osteoporosis
  • 7. Endocrine manifestation (↑ catabolism-> ↓ hormone levels)
  • -F: Ovulation may be impaired, oligomenorrhea/ secondary amenorrhea.
  • ↓ sex hormones
  • -M: Erectile dysfunction and gynecomastia.
  • 8. Skin and hair: warm, moist, and pink skin (cutaneous vasodilation and excessive sweating),
  • blushing; the hair= fine and friable, hair loss; the nails= soft and friable.
  • 9. Eye signs (due to ↑ adrenergic activity-> can be seen in all forms of hyperthyroidism):
  • Retraction of the upper/lower eyelids-> typical stare of the patient, lid lag (the upper lid lags
  • behind the globe when shifting the gaze downward), globe lag (the eye lags behind the upper
  • lid when the patient looks up), fine tremor of the lightly closed lids (Rosenbach’s sign).
  • Graves’ disease- particularities
  • -The goiter is diffuse, symmetrical, with a smooth surface; it can be soft/ firm and rubbery; in
  • severe cases, a thrill may be felt+ audible bruit.
  • -Ophthalmopathy (autoimmune mechanism-> cytokines released by lymphocytes sensitized to
  • the TSH receptor-> activation and proliferation of orbital fibroblasts and preadipocytes->↑
  • retro-orbital fat+ GAG deposition (extraocular muscles+ retro-orbital space)-> diplopia and
  • proptosis; proinflammatory cytokines also lead to redness, congestion, chemosis, periorbital
  • edema): irritation in the eyes, excessive tearing, exophthalmos (>18 mm) periorbital edema,
  • extraocular muscle dysfunction (double vision), photophobia, chemosis, scleral injection,
  • retrobulbar pressure/ pain, exposure keratitis, and optic neuropathy.
  • -Thyroid dermopathy (pretibial myxedema)- thickening of the skin, nonpitting edema over the
  • lower tibia or on the dorsum of the feet, hyperpigmentation.
  • !! Graves’ disease can be associated with other diseases such as DM type 1, Addison disease,
  • vitiligo, celiac disease, and myasthenia gravis.
  • Graves’ ophthalmopathy- Clinical Activity Score (CAS)
  • Activity measurement is based on the classical features of inflammation= the sum of
  • all items present:
  •  Spontaneous retrobulbar pain
  •  Pain on attempted up or downgaze
  •  Redness of the eyelids
  •  Redness of the conjunctiva
  •  Swelling of the eyelids
  •  Inflammation of the caruncle and/or plica
  •  Conjunctival edema (chemosis)
  • A CAS ≥3/7 indicates active GO

Graves’ ophthalmopathy- Werner’s classification of eye changes #3

  • • Class 0 (N): No signs or symptoms
  • • Class 1 (O): Only signs, no symptoms (lid retraction, lid lag, globe lag)
  • • Class 2 (S): Soft tissue involvement: periorbital edema, irritation, excessive tearing,
  • chemosis, enlarged lacrimal glands, proptosis <22 mm
  • • Class 3 (P): Proptosis ≥22 mm
  • • Class 4 (E): Extraocular muscle involvement (edema->fibrosis)—ophthalmoplegia->diplopia.
  • Upward gaze limitation= most common physical finding in patients with eye muscle
  • involvement. Another common finding is a convergence defect.
  • • Class 5 (C): Corneal involvement (keratitis) due to inability to close the eyes completely
  • = lagophthalmos (proptosis >32 mm)
  • • Class 6 (S): Sight loss -optic nerve involvement (ischemia of the nerve due to compression)
  • Hyperthyroidism- investigations
  • 1. Thyroid function tests - ↑FT4+ ↓ TSH= the diagnosis of primary hyperthyroidism
  • Exceptions: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma↑ TSH+ ↑FT4; T3-toxicosis FT3↑, FT4-N + TSH↓
  • 2. Thyroid ultrasonography
  • -Graves’ disease—diffuse thyroid hypertrophy, homogenous, hypoechoic; hypervascularization
  • -Toxic adenoma/toxic multinodular goiter—one nodule/enlarged gland that is diffusely
  • inhomogeneous with multiple individual nodules.
  • 3. Thyroid autoantibodies
  •  TRAb- highly specific for Graves’ disease
  •  TPO and TG antibodies- present in Graves’ disease and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.
  • 4. Other tests: N/ ↑ Glycaemia, ↓ Cholesterol, N/ ↑Alkaline phosphatase
  • 5. RAIU+ radionucleotide thyroid scan- employed if diagnosis= uncertain
  • ↑ RAIU is present in thyrotoxicosis with hyperthyroidism: Graves’ disease, toxic adenoma, and
  • toxic multinodular goiter.
  • - Thyroid scintigraphy (123I or 99Technetium scan) appearance:
  • (a) Graves’ disease- enlarged gland, usually symmetric, homogenous distribution of tracer
  • (b) Toxic adenoma- “hot” nodule with ↓ or absent function of the contralateral lobe.
  • (c) Toxic multinodular goiter- multiple functioning (“hot”) nodules in the gland.
  • 6. Ultrasonography, CT, and MRI scan of the orbits- extraocular muscle enlargement in most
  • patients with Graves’ disease.
  • 7. ECG: Sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, LV hypertrophy.

Hyperthyroidism- complications #4

  • (a) Thyrotoxic crisis (“thyroid storm”) = acute exacerbation of all the symptoms and signs of
  • thyrotoxicosis= LIFE-THREATENING CONDITION
  • - patient presents with fever (38–41 °C), flushing and sweating, cardiac arrhythmias, heart
  • failure, diarrhea, vomiting, marked agitation, delirium, and coma.
  • - treatment: ATDs+ Lugol solution+ Hydrocortisone hemisuccinate+ beta-blockers
  • (b) Thyrotoxic cardiac involvement (cardiothyreosis)- cardiac arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation),
  • heart failure, and myocardial ischemia.
  • (c) Thyrotoxic myopathy appears in severe untreated cases
  • (d) Thyrotoxic osteoporosis
  • (e) Diabetes mellitus
  • (f) Thyrotoxic hepatopathy (hepatic dysfunction)-particularly when thyrotoxicosis is severe.
  • Hyperthyroidism- treatment
  • 1. Medical Treatment= ATDs- interfere with the synthesis of T4 and T3 within the thyroid
  • gland+ immunosuppressive effects
  •  Imidazole Derivates
  • Thiamazole (Thyrozol) A typical regimen starts with larger doses (30–40 mg dose) for
  • Carbimazole 1–2 months-> reduced gradually to 5–10 mg for maintenance.
  •  Thiouracil Derivates
  • Methylthiouracil
  • Propylthiouracil- also blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion (may have advantages when given
  • at high doses in severe thyrotoxicosis).
  • Monitoring: serum FT4 and FT3 (TSH levels often remain suppressed for many weeks/ months)
  • Side effects of ATDs: Rash (managed with antihistamines), agranulocytosis (= indication for
  • discontinuing the medication), cholestatic jaundice with thiamazole, hepatocellular toxicity
  • with PTU, acute arthritis (= indication for cessation of therapy), hypothyroidism with goiter,
  • aplasia cutis (methimazole)-> PTU is preferred in pregnancy during the 1st trimester
  • 2. Other Medical Measures
  • • Rest
  • • Beta-adrenergic blocking agents: propranolol 10–40 mg every 6 h or longer-acting beta-
  • blockers: metoprolol and atenolol—for adrenergic symptoms, tachycardia and hypertension
  • • Sedatives
  • • Multivitamins

3. Surgical Treatment #5

  • Total thyroidectomy= the operation of choice
  • Preparation: ATDs until euthyroid (~ 6 weeks) + Lugol solution (~ 2 weeks before the day of
  • operation) 3 × 3 drops daily → 3 × 15 drops/day to↓ hyperplasia and hypervascularity
  • Complications : hypothyroidism (all patients should receive treatment with levothyroxine at
  • home after surgery!!), hypoparathyroidism, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
  • 4. Radioactive Iodine Therapy
  • Radioactive iodine (3–10 mCi 131I- typically given orally as a single capsule)
  • Side Effects: hypothyroidism (almost inevitable), anterior neck pain (radiation-induced
  • thyroiditis), development/exacerbation of eye problems-prevented by administration of
  • prednisone 40–60 mg/day for 1–2 months (gradually tapering the dose) after radioiodine
  • Contraindications: pregnant and lactating women, severe ophthalmopathy, young children
  • (potential risk of thyroid carcinogenesis)
  • Graves’ Ophthalmopathy- treatment
  • A. Medical treatment
  • 1. Stop Smoking
  • 2. Symptomatic treatment: - dark glasses, artificial tears, keeping the patient’s head elevated
  • at night+ diuretics- may help diminish periorbital edema.
  • - selenium (100 μgx2 daily) may improve symptoms in patients with mild forms.
  • 3. Glucocorticoids:
  • (a) Intravenous methylprednisolone (fewer side effects than with high doses of prednisone)
  • - 500 mg/week for 6 weeks-> 250 mg/week for another 6 weeks- moderate-severe forms OR
  • - pulse therapy 1 g/day for 3 days- very severe cases (sight-threatening)
  • (b) Prednisone 50–60 mg/day, tapering the dose 10 mg every 2 weeks until stop.
  • B. External radiation to the retrobulbar area (1000 cGy/orbit delivered over 10 fractions)
  • - helpful if corticosteroid therapy is not effective or contraindicated
  • - contraindicated in patients with hypertensive/diabetic retinopathy
  • !!Treatment with both radiotherapy and glucocorticoids is more effective than either alone.
  • C. Surgical Treatment
  • Surgical orbital decompression- in very severe cases when vision is threatened
  • Surgery for Strabismus- performed after any necessary orbital decompression and when eyes
  • are in a quiescent phase for at least 6 months after active disease
  • - aims to allow correct binocular vision
  • Eyelid Surgery- the final stage of any surgical approach- aims to adjust upper and lower eyelid
  • position.

Hypothyroidism- causes #6

  • - Inherited defects in hormone biosynthesis (e.g. Pendred syndrome- goiter+ hearing
  • loss)
  • - Hashimoto’s thyroiditis=by far the most common cause in the developed world
  • With
  • - Iodine deficiency (endemic goiter)
  • goiter - Excessive iodide intake (radiocontrast dye, amiodarone)- Wolf Chaikoff effect
  • - Drugs: interferon alfa, lithium
  • - Thyroid agenesis/ ectopic thyroid (lingual thyroid)- ascertained by scintiscanning
  • No
  • - Hashimoto’s disease
  • goiter
  • - Postablative due to 131I (radioactive iodine therapy), surgery
  • - Subacute thyroiditis
  • Transien
  • - Postpartum, silent thyroiditis

  • Hypothyroidism- clinical picture- adults
  • • Skin: cool, rough, dry, pale skin, cold sensitivity, puffy face, hands, feet (nonpitting edema);
  • yellowish skin color (↓conversion of carotene to vit. A), macroglossia, macrocheilia
  • • Hair: head and body hair- dry, brittle, tends to fall out; Hertoghe sign (eyebrows)
  • • Nails: brittle and grow slowly
  • • Digestive manifestations: ↓ appetite, peristalsis is markedly slowed->chronic constipation
  • and occasionally severe fecal impaction or ileus.
  • • Neuromuscular system: numbness, tingling of the extremities, muscle cramps and weakness
  • • Central and peripheral nervous system : ↓ in all intellectual functions-> bradylalia,
  • bradypsychia, hearing loss, loss of initiative, memory deficits, lethargy and somnolence;
  • psychiatric disorders are common: depression or agitation (“myxedema madness”)
  • • Reproductive function (in primary hypothyroidism- ↑TRH-> ↑PRL):
  • F- menorrhagia, anovulatory cycles, infertility, and galactorrhea
  • M- decreased libido, impotence, and oligospermia
  • • Cardiovascular signs: ↓ ventricular contraction, bradycardia, ↓cardiac output, ↑peripheral
  • resistance-> convergent BP formula (↑ DBP, ↓SBP); diminished heart sounds +/- pericardial
  • effusion.
  • • Respiratory signs: hoarseness (MPS deposition in the larynx), shallow, slow respirations and
  • impaired ventilatory responses to hypercapnia or hypoxia-> dyspnea and obstructive sleep
  • apnea.
  • • Renal function- ↓ glomerular filtration rate and impaired ability to excrete a water load.

!!Hashimoto’s thyroiditis may associate other endocrine autoimmune disorders e.g. #7

  • autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 = Schmidt’s syndrome (Addison’s+ Thyroid
  • autoimmune disease and/or DM 1)
  • Hypothyroidism- investigations
  • 1.Thyroid function tests- ↓ FT4+ ↑ TSH= diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism
  • Exception: Central hypothyroidism: ↓ FT4 + ↓/N TSH
  • 2.Thyroid Autoantibodies- anti-TG and anti-TPO- high titers in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.
  • 3.Other tests: ↑CK, LDH, AST, ALT, ↑ LDL-c, ↑ TGs, anemia, ↑ PRL (↑ TRH stimulates PRL
  • secretion)
  • 4.Thyroid ultrasonography- N, ↑or ↓ thyroid volume+ hypoechogenic aspect in Hashimoto’s
  • 5. RAIU+ thyroid scintigraphy- for assessing inherited defects in hormone biosynthesis,
  • thyroid agenesis, or ectopic thyroid gland.
  • 6. ECG: low-voltage of QRS complexes, P and T waves; prolongation of the QT and PR intervals,
  • sinus bradycardia; rarely complete heart block; alterations of the ST segment
  • 7. Thoracic X-ray may reveal cardiac enlargement.
  • 8. Echocardiography is useful in detecting the pericardial effusion.
  • Hypothyroidism- complications
  • 1. Myxedema coma with progressive weakness, stupor, hypothermia (T < 35 °C),
  • hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hypoventilation-> shock and death. Pleural, pericardial, or
  • abdominal effusions with high protein content may be present.
  • May be triggered by cold exposure, trauma, infection, and administration of CNS depressants.
  • 2. Myxedema cardiomyopathy -> congestive heart failure
  • 3. Myxedema pericarditis (pericardial effusion= rarely sufficient to cause tamponade).
  • 4. Coronary artery disease- related to high levels of total cholesterol and LDL-cholesterol.
  • 5. Myopathy.
  • 6. In newborn infant: Impairment of linear growth- disproportionate dwarfism (US/LS>1),
  • retardation of mental and physical development.
  • Hypothyroidism- treatment
  • • Euthyrox ( levothyroxine) 50–100 (200) μg/day (1.6 μg/kg)
  • !!The half-life of T4 is about 7 days-> given only once daily, 30 min before breakfast with water
  • for an optimal absorption; no other drugs should be taken at least 30 min after Euthyrox.
  • • Novothyral® (a combination L-T4/T3: 100 μg LT4 + 20 μg T3/tb)
  • Considerations:
  • - Usually the replacement therapy is for life, except for transient forms.
  • -The initial dose: depends on the degree of hypothyroidism, age and general health. In older
  • patients or patients with underlying heart disease- start with a low dose (e.g. 12.5-25 μg/day)
  • and increase slowly (at 1–2 week intervals) with careful clinical and laboratory evaluation.

- The dose should be ↑ by 25 μg in any woman on replacement therapy who is pregnant. #8

  • Monitoring: in primary hyperthyroidism TSH should be evaluated 6 weeks after a theoretically
  • completed replacement dose has been instituted. Once stabilized, check TSH annually.
  • Thyroid ultrasonography- normal thyroid gland
  • Thyroid ultrasonography -Basedow Graves
